content: People with asthma are at an increased risk of developing severe complications from influenza, even if their asthma is mild or well-controlled with medication. Asthma causes the airways to become inflamed and sensitive, and influenza can exacerbate this inflammation, leading to further airway and lung irritation. Influenza can trigger asthma attacks and worsen asthma symptoms. Additionally, individuals with asthma are more likely to develop pneumonia and other acute respiratory illnesses after contracting influenza compared to those without asthma. Among children hospitalized with influenza, asthma is the most common underlying medical condition, and it is also one of the more frequent conditions among adults hospitalized with influenza. Asthma is a chronic lung disease characterized by persistent inflammation of the airways. It is one of the most prevalent long-term conditions in children, though adults can also have asthma. Asthma attacks occur when the airways become swollen and constricted due to inflammation, often triggered by factors such as respiratory infections, allergens, chemical irritants, or air pollution. Symptoms of an asthma attack include wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and coughing, particularly at night or in the early morning. Preventing asthma attacks often involves avoiding known triggers and adhering to prescribed asthma medications. Annual influenza vaccination is crucial for individuals with asthma, as they are at higher risk of severe flu-related complications. The flu vaccine is updated annually to match circulating virus strains, and immunity from the vaccine develops approximately two weeks after administration. Vaccination not only reduces the risk of contracting influenza but also decreases the severity of illness in those who do contract the virus. Studies have shown that flu vaccination lowers the likelihood of hospitalization and intensive care unit (ICU) admission due to influenza. The CDC recommends that everyone aged six months and older receive a flu vaccine each year, ideally by the end of October. Most injectable flu vaccines are safe and approved for individuals with asthma, including children as young as six months. However, the nasal spray flu vaccine (live attenuated influenza vaccine, or LAIV) is generally not recommended for people with asthma. Children aged 2 to 4 years with asthma or a history of wheezing in the past year should not receive the nasal spray vaccine. Individuals with asthma should also ensure they are up to date with pneumococcal vaccinations, as pneumococcal pneumonia is a serious flu-related complication. Pneumococcal vaccines protect against diseases such as pneumonia, meningitis, and bloodstream infections. Consult your healthcare provider to determine which pneumococcal vaccine is appropriate for you. In addition to vaccination, individuals with asthma should follow everyday preventive measures to reduce the risk of influenza. These include avoiding contact with sick individuals, covering coughs, washing hands frequently, and maintaining clean and hygienic environments. People with asthma should also adhere to their prescribed asthma management plans, including taking medications as directed, avoiding known triggers, and keeping an adequate supply of medications. An updated written Asthma Action Plan, developed with a healthcare provider, should be followed for daily management and during asthma exacerbations. For children with asthma, ensure their Asthma Action Plan is on file at school or daycare, and that medications are readily accessible. If individuals with asthma develop flu symptoms, they should contact their healthcare provider promptly. Antiviral medications can treat influenza and reduce the risk of severe complications. Symptoms of influenza include fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, body aches, headache, chills, and fatigue. Some individuals, particularly children, may also experience vomiting and diarrhea. Antiviral drugs work by inhibiting the replication of influenza viruses in the body, making the illness milder and shortening its duration. These medications are most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. However, individuals with asthma should avoid the antiviral drug zanamivir (Relenza®), as it may cause wheezing or exacerbate respiratory issues. Emergency medical care should be sought immediately if individuals with asthma experience any of the following warning signs of severe flu complications: In children: Rapid or labored breathing Bluish lips or face Retraction of the ribs with each breath Chest pain Severe muscle pain (e.g., refusal to walk) Dehydration (e.g., no urine for 8 hours, dry mouth, absence of tears when crying) Lethargy or lack of responsiveness Seizures Fever above 104°F that does not respond to medication Any fever in children younger than 12 weeks Symptoms that improve but then worsen (e.g., fever or cough) Worsening of chronic medical conditions In adults: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath Persistent chest or abdominal pain Persistent dizziness, confusion, or unresponsiveness Seizures Lack of urination Severe muscle pain or weakness Symptoms that improve but then worsen (e.g., fever or cough) Worsening of chronic medical conditions These lists are not exhaustive. Any severe or concerning symptoms should prompt immediate consultation with a healthcare provider.
